question: What is the primary physical characteristic of an ovarian cyst?

options.A: A fluid-filled sac within or on an ovary
options.B: An inflamed thickening of the fallopian tube
options.C: An abnormal overgrowth of uterine lining
options.D: A solid mass of fibrous scar tissue

explanation: Ovarian cysts are specifically defined as fluid-filled pouches that develop on or inside the ovarian tissue during cyclical hormonal fluctuations. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h1)

question: Why do most functional ovarian cysts form during a normal menstrual cycle?

options.A: Blockage of the cervical os preventing normal blood flow
options.B: Excessive production of testosterone by the adrenal glands
options.C: Bacterial invasion of the ovarian cortex during ovulation
options.D: Failure of a follicle to rupture or reabsorb fluid properly

explanation: Functional cysts arise when developing follicles either do not release their egg or fail to dissolve after ovulation, causing fluid to pool inside. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h1)

question: Which type of ovarian cyst is known to contain embryonic tissues like hair and teeth?
explanation: Dermoid cysts develop from germ cells and frequently contain differentiated tissues such as hair, skin structures, and teeth. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h2)

question: How does an endometrioma differ structurally from a functional follicular cyst?

options.A: Endometriomas contain ectopic uterine tissue and old blood
options.B: Follicular cysts develop from surface epithelial cell mutations
options.C: Follicular cysts are composed entirely of dense solid cartilage
options.D: Endometriomas only form after complete surgical menopause

explanation: Endometriomas arise from misplaced endometrial tissue responding to hormonal cycles, characteristically filling with dark chocolate-like old blood. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h2)

question: What is the primary diagnostic imaging tool used to visualize ovarian cysts?
explanation: Pelvic ultrasound provides safe, non-invasive imaging that accurately differentiates between fluid-filled cysts and solid ovarian masses. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h3)

question: Why might a clinician order a serum CA-125 blood test for a patient with an ovarian mass?

options.A: To assess blood clotting times prior to emergency cyst surgery
options.B: To measure circulating progesterone levels during the luteal phase
options.C: To confirm the presence of an acute bacterial pelvic infection
options.D: To evaluate the possibility of underlying ovarian malignancy

explanation: CA-125 is a tumor marker often elevated in epithelial ovarian cancers, helping guide the evaluation of suspicious adnexal masses. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h3)

question: Which of the following is the standard initial approach for a small, asymptomatic functional ovarian cyst?
explanation: Because most functional cysts disappear on their own within a few cycles, conservative monitoring is the preferred first step. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h4)

question: A patient with a recurrent functional ovarian cyst asks if birth control pills will shrink her current mass. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Hormonal contraceptives will dissolve the current cyst within one week.
options.B: Contraceptives prevent future ovulation but do not shrink existing cysts.
options.C: Birth control pills are the primary surgical alternative to laparoscopy.
options.D: Oral contraceptives must be stopped immediately to avoid cyst rupture.

explanation: Hormonal suppression stops new functional cysts from developing, but it has no proven effect on accelerating the reabsorption of an already formed cyst. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h4)

question: What is the primary pathophysiological event in ovarian torsion?

options.A: Malignant transformation of surface epithelial cells
options.B: Infection of the fallopian tubes by ascending bacteria
options.C: Rupture of an endometrial implant into the peritoneal cavity
options.D: Twisting of the ovary on its vascular pedicle cutting off blood supply

explanation: Ovarian torsion happens when the weight of a cyst causes the ovary to rotate, twisting blood vessels and cutting off oxygen supply. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h5)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of acute ovarian torsion rather than a simple asymptomatic cyst?

options.A: Gradual weight gain over several months
options.B: Sudden, severe, unilateral lower abdominal pain with vomiting
options.C: Bilateral lower extremity edema and pallor

explanation: The acute ischemia caused by a twisted vascular pedicle triggers sharp, severe localized pain accompanied by autonomic signs like nausea and vomiting. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h5)

question: Which instruction is most vital to include when educating a patient discharged with a managed ovarian cyst?

options.A: Avoid all physical activity for the remainder of your life
options.B: Report sudden, severe pelvic pain or dizziness immediately
options.C: Perform daily self-administered vaginal ultrasounds at home
options.D: Stop taking prescribed pain medications once spotting begins

explanation: Patients must recognize warning signs of complications like torsion or rupture so they can seek urgent care without delay. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h6)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility during the conservative management phase of an ovarian cyst?

options.A: Insisting on immediate surgical removal regardless of size
options.B: Administering intravenous chemotherapy to prevent malignancy
options.C: Performing manual bedside cyst drainage procedures
options.D: Tracking follow-up ultrasound appointments and monitoring pain

explanation: Conservative management requires vigilant monitoring of symptom changes and ensuring the patient attends scheduled imaging to track cyst resolution. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T32#GNS216_U5_T32_h6)
